no_point_fails.reason: A clean point can be written: check that a documented assessment justifies whether finishing operations need dedicated facilities, considering the A8 factors, the product's specific needs and the other products (including non-biological ones) in the facility.

Despite the 'may be divided' wording, inspectors treat a separate solution preparation area as an expected room for FFS/BFS LVP manufacture, and its absence would draw a major finding; a point such as 'Verify a separate solution preparation area/room is provided for FFS/BFS LVP manufacture' can be checked by observation and layout drawings.

Although framed as 'may be divided', a clean point can be written ('Is a separate quarantine area provided for parenteral preparations in glass containers?'), and its absence would likely draw a major finding for mix-up risk with unreleased sterile product.
A clean point can be written: verify that the MAH's shortage prevention and mitigation risk assessments consider the potential patient harm from product unavailability, as linked in ICH Q9.

Missing de-gowning and decontamination procedures in a cytotoxic or hormone containment facility would likely draw a major finding, so this unit should be an audit point (e.g., 'Are documented, appropriate de-gowning and decontamination procedures established and followed for the containment area?').

A clean point can be written: check that changes during IMP development are documented and justified (e.g., change control or product specification file) and that consistency between batches used in the same or different trials is shown; undocumented changes would likely be a major finding.
A clean point is possible: where site-to-site IMP transfers may occur, check that the technical agreement defines the requirements and responsibilities for this exceptional transfer process.

The parenthetical sets a checkable QP duty, so a point could be written: for investigational combined ATMPs whose device is itself investigational, check that batch certification records show the QP verified the device against the manufacturer's quality specifications.

The unit implies a checkable duty, which is the only place in this block requiring critical equipment qualification, and unqualified critical equipment or an unvalidated process would draw a major finding; write a point such as 'Verify critical equipment is qualified, the process is validated and changes are controlled for phytopharmaceuticals with unknown active constituents.'

The unit sets the minimum grade D background for closed-system and isolator production, so it can be audited by checking room classification and EM records for those areas, and an unclassified background without 9.45 justification would be a major finding.

A clean audit point can be written: check the APS protocols and records to confirm that units removed after aseptic set-up or mandatory line clearances were incubated separately and their results evaluated.

Though worded as an example, this is checkable by reviewing the technical agreements: where the sponsor relies on a chain of contracted manufacturers, do they specify each manufacturer's exact tasks and GMP/GDP responsibilities? Undefined roles in such a chain would likely draw a major finding.

Manufacturing that does not comply with the Marketing/Clinical Trial Authorisation is a typical major or critical finding, and it can be checked by comparing batch records, specifications and processes against the MA/CTA dossier.

This is checkable and major (risk of mislabelled or adulterated materials, e.g. DEG-contaminated excipients from traders): a point can verify that the reduced identity-sampling procedure is not applied to starting materials from brokers or intermediaries whose manufacturer is unknown or unaudited, and that each container of such materials is identity-tested.

Although listed under 'may include', QP review of batch records (control, in-process and release reports) against the PSF, order, protocol and randomisation code is a core certification element; omitting it would be a major finding, and it can be audited from QP certification checklists and batch review records.

A clean audit point can be written: check the HVAC design and pressure monitoring records to confirm that areas where radioactive products are exposed are at lower pressure than surrounding areas where containment requires it.

This is checkable: verify that the IMP technical agreement forbids subcontracting agreed responsibilities without the contract giver's prior evaluation and approval, and that any subcontractors were approved; unapproved subcontracting is a major Chapter 7 finding.

Pressure is a recognised critical EO cycle parameter, and failing to validate and monitor it would likely draw a major finding. A clean point can be written: verify that chamber pressure is defined as a CPP in EO sterilisation validation and is recorded for each routine cycle.

A clean point can be written: check that OQ records document that critical equipment performs as intended across its anticipated operating ranges, and lacking OQ for critical equipment is typically a major finding.

Though phrased as a benefit, the unit describes a checkable state: an audit point could verify, through documents and interview, that the MAH holds adequate knowledge of the manufacturing processes, impurity formation and related controls at the finished product and active substance sites.

A clean point can be written: check that the documented dedicated-versus-campaign decision for formulation and filling considers the biological product's characteristics, the other products including non-biologicals, and the filling technology used (e.g. single-use closed systems).

Though phrased as 'can', this is checkable: a point could verify that MAH-held data (complaints, recalls, MA variations, post-marketing commitments) actually appear in the PQR, by cross-checking PQR reports against MAH records.

A clean point can be written: check that the job descriptions of the heads of production, QC and (where applicable) QA assign the listed shared PQS responsibilities (training, documentation, process, transport and reconstitution validation, environmental control, outsourced activities, investigations).

A clean point can be written: check that documented OQ shows critical equipment, as installed or modified, performs as intended across its anticipated operating ranges. Missing or inadequate OQ of critical equipment would likely draw a major finding.

Temperature is a fundamental EO critical process parameter, so a point should check that it is defined in validation and monitored and recorded for each routine cycle; an uncontrolled cycle temperature would be a major finding.

This is the operative limit for non-threshold genotoxic residual actives and is checkable in the HBEL/cleaning-limit assessment (verify the limit is the 1.5 µg/person/day TTC unless a compound-specific acceptable intake is justified); an unjustified higher limit would be a major cross-contamination finding.

Exposure time is a core critical parameter of EO sterilisation, and an uncontrolled exposure time would draw a major finding. It can be audited cleanly: check that exposure time is defined and validated as a CPP and recorded in each cycle's routine monitoring records.

A point can be written to check that starting materials for parenteral products are excluded from any reduced-sampling or identity-test exemption, with every container identity-tested. Skipping this for parenteral materials would likely draw a major finding.

A clean point can be written: check that the recall procedure, and past recall records, allow a recall to be started to protect public or animal health before the root cause and full extent of the defect are established.

Indian inspectors treat the Part XIII parenteral area list as the expected layout, and having no segregated solution preparation/filtration room would draw a major finding; it can be checked from layout drawings and a site walk as 'solution preparation and filtration are done in a separate designated area/room'.

Monitoring staff exposure levels is checkable through industrial hygiene and exposure monitoring records, and having none in a hormone or cytotoxic facility would likely be a major finding, so it should be an audit point (e.g. 'Verify that industrial hygiene monitoring of staff exposure levels is performed and recorded').

A clean point can be written: check that a medical surveillance programme monitoring staff exposure levels exists and is recorded for personnel handling hazardous substances, as determined by the facility's containment approach.

A clean point can be checked by observation and records: are suitable radioactivity measurement equipment (e.g. dose calibrators) and radioactive reference standards available where needed, since lacking them would be a major finding.

A conditional point can be written: where ATMPs are released before all QC tests are complete, check that the QP's initial certification for administration is preceded by a documented review of batch processing records, environmental monitoring results and available analytical results. Releasing without this review would be a major finding.
A clean point can be written: check that, where the initial three-batch validation gave limited data, the validation report or OPV plan defines supplementary data collection from subsequent batches.

A clean point is possible and needed: check that the technical agreement defines how proposed changes to manufacturing and control methods are communicated between manufacturer and sponsor, since an undocumented change process risks unauthorised deviation from the approved CTA (a likely major finding).

Cleaning procedures are not optional: 9.35#9-#12 require adapted, risk-based, validated cleaning between every batch, so a missing cleaning procedure would be a major finding and a clean point can be written, e.g. 'documented adequate cleaning/decontamination procedures exist for production areas and equipment'.

A clean point can be written: check that the technical agreement or other documented arrangement keeps TMF-relevant IMP documentation (QP batch certification, packaging records, CoA) available to the sponsor after the GMP retention period ends, as Article 58 of Regulation (EU) 536/2014 requires.

Documenting management review results and actions, communicating them on time and escalating issues to senior management can be checked in the review minutes, action trackers and distribution or escalation records, and an inspector would likely raise a major finding if they were missing, so this should be an audit point.

Inspectors routinely check that specifications reflect the current IP or official pharmacopoeia edition, and outdated monographs are a typical major finding, so write a point such as 'Specifications are revised when new pharmacopoeia editions are issued, verified by edition references and revision history'.

A clean point can be written: check that the technical agreement, where applicable, defines responsibility for sourcing authorised (e.g. comparator) products from an authorised vendor and for recall arrangements, verified against the agreement and supplier records.

A clean point can be written: for IMP processes such as mixing that are not validated, check the batch records for additional QC testing (e.g. blend uniformity) or a documented justification for not doing it.
A clean audit point can be written: verify that the manufacturer–sponsor technical agreement defines the un-blinding arrangements and each party's responsibilities for blinded IMPs.

A clean point can be written: check that personnel protection measures matching the known risks of the product and materials (e.g. biosafety PPE or containment for viral vectors) are defined and applied, the same conditional way as the vaccination point 3.33#2.

A clean point can be written: check supplier performance and monitoring records to verify that suppliers or service providers showing substantial variability in material quality or safety were placed under enhanced review and monitoring.

Manufacturing sites and QPs lacking visibility of the registered MA details and agreed regulatory commitments would likely draw a major finding, and this is checkable via technical agreements, MA summaries or commitment lists provided to the sites, and QP interview, so it should be an audit point.

Missing or inadequate PPE in hazardous/cytotoxic handling areas would draw a major finding, so this should be an audit point, e.g. verify that appropriate PPE is specified, provided and used as part of the containment controls.

Inspectors treat Part XIII as minimum facility requirements, and lacking a segregated area for washing and drying containers and closures in a parenteral plant would likely be a major finding; an observation point such as 'Is there a separate area for washing and drying ampoules, vials, bottles and closures?' can be written.

A clean point can be written (does the technical agreement assign who gives the QP the latest authorised CTA/IMPD information for batch certification?), and a QP certifying against outdated authorised documents would likely draw a major finding.

Although framed as a benefit, this is a checkable and significant duty: verify through technical agreements and change-notification records that manufacturing sites inform the MAH of changes affecting Modules 1–3, ASMFs or CEPs, since missing this leads to unapproved variations.

Relative humidity is a critical EO lethality parameter, and the audit point is checkable: verify that the EO validation report and routine cycle records define, monitor and keep RH within validated limits.

The permission carries a checkable condition, so a clean point can be written: where a PDE is used for a genotoxic active substance, verify the HBEL assessment documents sufficient evidence of a threshold-related mechanism.

Uncontrolled cross-contamination on shared purification equipment such as chromatography resins would likely draw a major finding, and a clean point can be written: for multi-product harvest and purification equipment, verify that additional controls (dedicated resins, additional testing) are in place where appropriate.

The 'can facilitate' wording is a benefit statement, but the means it names is checkable: an audit point can verify that the MAH has documented two-way communication arrangements (SOPs, technical agreements) with competent authorities, manufacturing sites, QPs and complaint/stability organisations.

A point could check that, for IMPs imported from a third country, the QP batch assessment includes documents showing the manufacturer is authorised by the third-country authority to manufacture IMP for export; certifying an import without this evidence would likely be a major finding.

A clean audit point can be written: check that the sponsor–manufacturer technical agreement defines who handles deviations (e.g. temperature excursions) during IMP shipment to trial sites, a core topic of this shipping guideline and checkable by document review.

Qualification and validation is a listed basic QC requirement, and missing qualification or validation of QC activities would be a major finding, so it should be an audit point checking the QC qualification/validation records.
A conditional point can be checked by walkthrough: sensitive instruments are housed in separate rooms where needed to protect them from vibration, electrical interference and humidity.

Although listed as an example, the content can be checked against documents: verify that the technical agreement, or other controlled documents, define and record the storage conditions and location of IMP reference and retention samples.

Although listed under 'may include as appropriate', a QP certifying IMP batches without verifying the supply chain (manufacturing, packaging, labelling and testing sites) would likely draw a major finding, consistent with the Annex 16 principles that ¶4#1 requires the QP to take account of. A clean point can be written: 'Where appropriate, does the QP batch assessment record verification of the supply chain, including manufacturing, packaging, labelling and testing sites?'
A clean audit point can be written: for investigational ATMPs whose trial will support an MAA, check that batch or process data demonstrate consistent production.

Repeatedly manufacturing outside the MA after a deviation without submitting a variation is a major finding, and it is checkable: write a point verifying that where deviation outcomes require the changed process to continue, a variation to the MA was submitted.

Although framed as 'may require', poor containment-focused facility design and layout for hazardous products is a likely major finding, and it can be checked by layout drawings and observation: 'Verify facility design and layout emphasise safe containment of the hazardous materials handled.'

Although phrased as a rationale, the clause implies that cell banks must undergo safety testing for adventitious agents and characterisation; missing testing would be a critical finding, and records of this testing can be checked as an audit point.

Cross-contamination on shared multiproduct fermentation or cell-culture equipment is a likely major finding, and the unit is checkable as a point: 'Is additional post-cleaning testing between product campaigns on shared equipment assessed and, where warranted, performed and recorded?'

Together with #12–#13, this clause can be checked: confirm that no reduced-sampling identity-testing exemption is applied to starting materials from brokers or unaudited sources or to materials for parenterals, which would otherwise be a major finding.

An inappropriately designed HVAC/ECS in a hazardous-substance containment facility would be a major finding, so this should be an audit point: verify that the HVAC/ECS design (e.g., qualification/design documents) is appropriate for containing the hazardous materials handled.

Inspectors treat the Part XIII area list as the expected layout, so a clean observation point can be written: verify that a separate, designated visual inspection area exists for FFS/BFS large volume parenteral manufacture.

A clean point can be written: check records that the MAH informed manufacturing sites of MA changes affecting them (e.g. package leaflet or specification changes), and failing to do so would likely be a major finding because batches would not comply with the MA.

A clean point can be written: check that starting-material files hold the needed source, origin, supply-chain, manufacturing-method and control (including microbiological quality) documentation where applicable; the 'may require' only scopes this to relevant materials.

Where ATMPs are released before testing is complete, QP final certification after the final analytical results is a must-have step that can be checked in batch records; missing it would be a major finding, so this needs its own audit point.
